subject: Francis of Assisi
note: One writer, research and writing in one pass (SAINT-BRIEF.md). Every fetched text is under design/saints-hub/sources/people/francis-of-assisi/ (gitignored). Celano (Howell 1908) and the Three Companions (Salter 1902) were copied from the kindred research's fetched texts (sources/kindred-sources/). OCR texts: quotations crossing a page heading, footnote mark or speaker's tag use `parts`; the Canticle uses `scan` (one line-break hyphen). Every quotation passes verify-quotes.mjs. Modern copyrighted works (Osipov in English, the Gospel Coalition, Renoux) are cited or quoted only in their own short words or paraphrased; no modern translation is quoted.

life.text: Born at Assisi in 1181 or 1182; father Pietro Bernardone, a wealthy cloth merchant; mother Pica; baptised Giovanni, renamed Francesco by his father; died there 3 October 1226 (Saturday evening), in his 45th year and the 20th of his conversion.
life.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1909), St. Francis of Assisi (by Paschal Robinson)

life.text: First named John by his mother; his father, in whose absence he was born, returned from France and he was then named Francis. Merry, free-handed, 'going round the city of Assisi day and night in company with his like'; his mother: 'What think ye of my son? He shall yet be the son of God by grace.'
life.source: Legend of the Three Companions, chapter 1 (section 2), tr. E. Gurney Salter (1902)

life.text: Captive at Perugia after a battle between Perugia and Assisi; laughed at his chains; 'I shall yet be worshipped as a Saint all the world over'; bore with a proud knight all shunned. Dates 1202-1203 from Howell's chronology; 'when the year was ended and peace made' (Three Companions 4).
life.source: Celano, Second Life, 4; Howell (1908), Principal dates; Three Companions, 4

life.text: Dream of a house full of arms ('saddles, shields, lances') where there used to be bales of cloth; set out for Apulia; at Spoleto a voice: 'Which can do the better for thee, the lord, or the servant?'; returned toward Assisi.
life.source: Celano, First Life, 5; Three Companions, 5-6

life.text: Stopped his nostrils at lepers' houses two miles off; met a leper and kissed him (1 Cel 17); riding near Assisi, the leper 'received money and a kiss with it', then 'he could not see that leper at all' (2 Cel 9); the Testament opens with the lepers.
life.source: Celano, First Life, 17; Second Life, 9; Testament (Robinson 1906)

life.text: Courtesy: rebuffed a poor man, then resolved to 'never in future deny anything to any one asking him for the sake of God'; 'for he was most courteous'.
life.source: Celano, First Life, 17

life.text: San Damiano crucifix: 'Francis, go repair My house, which as thou seest is wholly falling into ruin'. Sold scarlet cloths and the horse at Foligno (1 Cel 8); offered money to the priest of San Damiano (1 Cel 9); repaired San Damiano (1 Cel 18), then another church, then the Portiuncula (1 Cel 21).
life.source: Celano, Second Life, 10; First Life, 8, 9, 18, 21

life.text: Before the bishop: stripped 'stark naked before all the bystanders'; the bishop covered him with his mantle (1 Cel 15); 'Henceforth I may freely say our Father who art in heaven...' (2 Cel 12); bishop named Guido (1 Cel 32).
life.source: Celano, First Life, 12-15, 32; Second Life, 12

life.text: The Gospel of the mission at the Portiuncula, 'in the third year from his conversion': 'This is what I wish, this is what I am seeking...'; shoes off, staff down, a cord for a girdle.
life.source: Celano, First Life, 21-22

life.text: To Rome with the brethren to Innocent III (1 Cel 32-33); Howell's chronology: 1210, with eleven brethren; the CE gives 1209; Innocent's dream of the Lateran propped by 'a certain Religious, a man small and despised' (2 Cel 17). The name Lesser Brethren from the Rule's 'And be they lesser' (1 Cel 38).
life.source: Celano, First Life, 32-33, 38; Second Life, 17; Howell (1908), Principal dates

life.text: Clare leaves home the night after Palm Sunday 1212 by 'a door much barred and obstructed with stones', comes to the Portiuncula, her hair is cut; San Damiano. The 1910 book is Charlotte Balfour's English of a French version of 1563 of the Legend ascribed to Celano; OCR is poor, so only one short line is quoted.
life.source: The Life and Legend of the Lady Saint Clare (1910); Catholic Encyclopedia (1909)

life.text: Chapter of Mats, Porziuncola, Whitsuntide 1220 or 1221: 'about 5000 friars are said to have been present', sheltering in huts of wattle and mud.
life.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1909)

life.text: Rule of 1223: written at Fonte Colombo near Rieti, entrusted to Elias, who 'declared he had lost it through negligence'; rewritten in twelve chapters; approved by Honorius III on 29 November 1223; 'the one ever since professed throughout the First Order'.
life.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1909); Robinson (1906), introduction to the Rules

life.text: Rule of 1221, ch. 17: 'Nevertheless, let all the brothers preach by their works.' Rule of 1223, ch. 9: 'with brevity of speech because the Lord made His word short upon earth'. Rule of 1221, ch. 16: two ways among the Saracens.
life.source: The Writings of St Francis, tr. Paschal Robinson (1906)

life.text: Egypt 1219: 'the lofty purpose to attain martyrdom' (1 Cel 56); seized and beaten, 'most honourably received by the Soldan', offered gifts, 'He was deeply stirred by his words and heard him very willingly' (1 Cel 57). CE: sailed from Ancona, present at the siege of Damietta; Jacques de Vitry says the sultan received him with courtesy.
life.source: Celano, First Life, 56-57; Catholic Encyclopedia (1909)

life.text: Jacques de Vitry's letter of 1220 in Sabatier's English (Houghton 1894): 'The master of these Brothers is named Brother Francis; he is so lovable that he is venerated by everyone ... asked him in secret to entreat God to reveal to him, by some miracle, which is the best religion.' Sabatier doubts the fire story: 'We know how little such an appeal to signs is characteristic of St. Francis.'
life.source: Paul Sabatier, Life of St. Francis of Assisi (1894), tr. Louise Seymour Houghton

life.text: Bonaventure, Legenda Major 9.7-8: set out 'that by the shedding of his blood the Faith of the Trinity might be spread abroad'; companion Illuminato; offer to enter the fire; the Sultan: 'I do not believe that any of my priests would be ready to expose himself unto the fire...'; feared a revolt. Written by command of the Chapter of Narbonne, 1260 (Okey).
life.source: Bonaventure, Life of St Francis, tr. E. Gurney Salter, in the Everyman volume (1910)

life.text: The Sultan's name, al-Malik al-Kamil, is not in the fetched early sources (they say 'the Soldan', 'the sultan, King of Egypt'); it is standard history (Wikipedia lead, 'known to have met with Saint Francis'), used only in the circle card.
life.source: Wikipedia, Al-Kamil (lead only)

life.text: Chesterton (1923), chapter 6: 'he treated the whole mob of men as a mob of kings'; chapter 8: 'it broke off short like the beginnings of a great bridge that might have united East and West, and remains one of the great might-have-beens of history'.
life.source: G. K. Chesterton, St. Francis of Assisi (1923), Project Gutenberg 63084

life.text: Greccio, Christmas 'in the third year before the day of his glorious decease' (1223): John of Greccio; 'about fifteen days before the Nativity'; manger, hay, ox and ass; tapers and torches; Mass over the manger; 'he was a Levite' and sang the Gospel; 'Bethlehem' 'in the manner of a sheep bleating'; a man saw a child in the manger in a vision. No figures of Mary or Joseph are mentioned.
life.source: Celano, First Life, 84-86

life.text: Stigmata: at Alverna two years before his death, the vision of a seraph fixed to a cross; 'marks of nails began to appear in his hands and feet'; the side wound bled; Elias saw it, Rufino touched it; he 'concealed the stigmata most diligently from strangers' (1 Cel 94-95). At death: 'not the prints of the nails but the nails themselves formed out of his flesh and retaining the blackness of iron' (1 Cel 113).
life.source: Celano, First Life, 94-95, 112-113

life.text: Brother Leo's note on the Assisi sheet: a Lent on La Verna from the Assumption to Michaelmas, two years before his death; 'after the vision and speech of the Seraph and the impression of the Stigmata of Christ in his body he made and wrote with his own hand the Praises'. Only two autographs known (the Assisi sheet; the Spoleto letter to Leo). The tau as his signature (Celano, Tractatus de miraculis; Bonaventure 4.3).
life.source: Paschal Robinson, The Writings of St Francis (1906)

life.text: Elias's circular letter (1226), in Sabatier's English: 'For a long time before his death our Brother and Father appeared as crucified, having in his body five wounds which are truly the stigmata of Christ'. Sabatier: the 'pious fraud' theory set aside (Leo, Angelo and Rufino, Elias's opponents, would be accomplices); 'They may have been a unique fact without being more miraculous than other phenomena'; Berlinghieri's Pescia portrait (Sabatier dates it 1236; the panel reads MCCXXXV) shows the stigmata; Gregory IX, 1237, Confessor Domini and two bulls to the Bishop of Olmütz and to the Dominicans for calling the stigmata in question.
life.source: Sabatier (1894), Critical study of the stigmata

life.text: Orthodox voices: the OCA's Q&A, 'Stigmata, such as manifested in Padre Pio, are foreign to the Orthodox experience and, as such, the Church has no official position'. A. I. Osipov (English translation on johnsanidopoulos.com, not quoted, being a modern translation): the stigmata are 'well known in psychiatry', nothing supernatural; the birds and wolf as prelest.
life.source: OCA, Questions and Answers, Manifestations; Osipov via John Sanidopoulos

life.text: Tamassia's charge that Celano composed 'a patchwork' from Gregory, Sulpicius Severus, Cassian and others (reported by Howell, who does not accept it in full).
life.source: A. G. Ferrers Howell, introduction to The Lives of S. Francis (1908)

life.text: Birds near Bevagna and the sermon; swallows at Alviano and 'Truly this man is a Saint, and a friend of the Most High' (1 Cel 58-59); fish thrown back (1 Cel 61); worms, bees fed honey or wine in winter (1 Cel 80); all creatures called brother (1 Cel 81); dancing before Honorius III (1 Cel 73); Otto IV passing Rivo Torto (1 Cel 43).
life.source: Celano, First Life

life.text: Brother Fire and the cautery from the ear to the eyebrow; 'I tell you, brethren, I have seen wondrous things to-day' (2 Cel 166). Wolves and hail at Greccio cease (2 Cel 35). Christmas on a Friday, 'the very walls should eat flesh' (2 Cel 199); grain for 'our sisters the larks' (2 Cel 200). Snow figures and 'brother ass' (2 Cel 116-117). Money like dung, the coin carried in the mouth (2 Cel 65). 'I know Christ, the poor man crucified' (2 Cel 105). Joy against the devil (2 Cel 125).
life.source: Celano, Second Life

life.text: The Canticle made at St Damian's, in a hut of reeds, September 1225 (CE); the verse on forgiveness added to reconcile the Bishop and the Podestà of Assisi, the Podestà's and the Bishop's words (Mirror of Perfection 101, compiled about 1318 from Leo's memoirs, per Okey). The Canticle is in Umbrian dialect rhyme (Robinson).
life.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1909); Mirror of Perfection, tr. Robert Steele; Okey's introduction; Robinson (1906)

life.text: Death: last days at the Porziuncola; bread broken; 'I have done my part...' (CE) / 'I have done my duty, may Christ teach you yours' (2 Cel 214); laid naked on the ground, covered the side wound with his hand (2 Cel 214); the Passion of John read, Psalm 141 (Vulgate; 142 in the BSB), died at 'Bring my soul out of prison' (CE), 'I cried unto the Lord with my voice' (1 Cel 109); 'Welcome, my sister Death' (2 Cel 217); Brother Jacoba admitted (CE); body borne on 4 October via St Damian's for Clare; San Giorgio; 25 May 1230 moved by Elias under the high altar; coffin found 12 December 1818 after 52 nights' search (CE). Larks at nightfall (Bonaventure 14.6).
life.source: Celano, Second Life, 214, 217; First Life, 108-110; Catholic Encyclopedia (1909); Bonaventure

life.text: Canonisation at Assisi by Gregory IX, 16 July 1228; the cardinals at Perugia: 'No need ... for miracles'; the decree 'that his festival be kept on the day of his death'; Celano wrote the First Life 'at the bidding of the lord and glorious Pope Gregory', 1228-29; the Second Life 1244-47; Celano admitted about 1213-1216.
life.source: Celano, First Life, preface, 119-126; Howell (1908), introduction

life.text: Subiaco fresco: 'Probably the oldest likeness ... It is said that it was painted by a Benedictine monk during the saint's visit there, which may have been in 1218. The absence of the stigmata, halo, and title of saint ... its chief claim to be considered a contemporary picture.' Legend of birth in a stable 'dates from the fifteenth century only'. Third Order of the Brothers and Sisters of Penance. 'Brother Ass', pardon asked of his body. 'Il Poverello'.
life.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1909)

life.text: Patron of ecology: Inter Sanctos, 29 November 1979 ('Sanctum Franciscum Assisiensem oecologiae cultorum Patronum caelestem renuntiamus'). Patron of animals and, with Catherine of Siena, of Italy (Britannica). Laudato si' (2015) opens with the Canticle's 'LAUDATO SI', mi' Signore'. William Draper's 'All Creatures of Our God and King', written around 1910 for a children's Whitsuntide festival in Leeds, published 1919 (Hymnary).
life.source: vatican.va; Britannica; Hymnary.org

life.text: Myths: 'Preach the Gospel at all times. Use words if necessary.' not in his writings or any biographer (The Gospel Coalition, FactChecker). The Peace Prayer: La Clochette no. 12, December 1912, anonymous; sent to Benedict XV 1915; Osservatore Romano 1916; printed about 1920 on the back of an image of St Francis without attribution; first attributed to him in 1927 (Les Chevaliers du Prince de la Paix); first known English 1936 (Kirby Page) (Christian Renoux). The Little Flowers: Italian of a Latin original compiled some time after 1322; Okey's brigand 'Fra Lupo' suggestion. Deacon: 'he resisted all efforts to persuade him to become a priest' (LFF 2022).
life.source: The Gospel Coalition; Franciscan Archive (Renoux); Okey (1910); Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022

life.text: Dante, Paradiso 11 (Longfellow): 'rose upon the world a sun'. Hallam's dismissal, quoted by Okey (1910): 'a harmless enthusiast, pious and sincere, but hardly of sane mind'.
life.source: Wikisource (Longfellow 1867); Okey (1910)

life.text: Pronunciation of Assisi: ə-ˈsi-sē, also -ˈsē-.
life.source: Merriam-Webster, Assisi

feasts.who: Catholic memorial ('4 S. Francisci Assisiensis', Memoria)
feasts.source: Calendarium Romanum (1969); USCCB Liturgical Calendar 2026 (Spanish list: '4 San Francisco de Asís'; 4 October 2026 is a Sunday, so the English day-by-day list omits it)

feasts.who: Church of England, Lesser Festival ('Francis of Assisi, Friar, Deacon, Founder of the Friars Minor, 1226', printed like Martin's lesser festival)
The Episcopal Church ('Francis of Assisi, Friar and Deacon, 1226'; 4 October is blank)
ELCA ('Francis of Assisi, renewer of the church, 1226')
feasts.source: Evangelical Lutheran Worship, the church year (2006 draft)

feasts.who: LCMS: not in the Lutheran Service Book commemorations
Impression of the Stigmata, 1916 Roman Martyrology; 1969: added 1585, suppressed 1602, restored 1615, left to particular calendars because it doubles the 4 October memorial
Translation of St Francis in the time of Gregory IX, 1916 Roman Martyrology (CE: 25 May 1230)
Orthodox: no Orthodox calendar keeps him (a Western saint canonised by Rome after 1054)
feasts.source: No entry in the OCA's lives of saints; stated as not on the calendar, with no claim of any conciliar ruling

pictures.size: original 1104 x 1152, saved as is at quality 84 (273 KB). Under the 1800 px aim: the only large clear scan of the face found; Cimabue_018/019/020 are the whole fresco or other details

Giotto, predella of the Stigmatization panel, the sermon to the birds, 1295-1300, Louvre
pictures.size: original 2765 x 3136, saved 1323 x 1500 at quality 83 (517 KB)

pictures.license: Public domain (Commons tag); the high-resolution Pescia photographs on Commons are CC BY-SA and were not used

could_not_verify: The Muslim side of 1219 beyond what the Christian writers report: the epitaph of Fakhr al-Din al-Farisi (Massignon's reading, disputed) could not be fetched from an open source, so the page does not mention it.
The Sultan's name (al-Malik al-Kamil) rests on standard history, not a fetched primary text; it appears only on the circle card.
Ignatius Brianchaninov's criticism of Francis's hagiographer (The Arena, ch. 11) exists only in modern copyrighted English; not used. Osipov is cited, not quoted.

The Subiaco painting's date: the CE (1909) reports 'said to have been painted ... during the saint's visit there, which may have been in 1218'; the Commons page (Polish text, after Le Goff) says 1228-1229. The page gives the CE's words with 'it is said'.
Clare's Life (1910) is an English version of a French version (1563) of the Latin legend; the OCR is poor. Only one short line is quoted.
The Peace Prayer's popular English first line is printed as the claim; its evidence is the 1912 French original (verify-quotes kind 'own').

checked: Dates and numbers against the texts on disk: born 1181 or 1182, died Saturday evening 3 October 1226 with Celano's 'Sunday the fourth day of October' (1 Cel 88), body carried up on 4 October via San Damiano, San Giorgio, moved 25 May 1230, coffin found 12 December 1818 after 'fifty-two nights' (CE); canonised 16 July 1228 (21 months); about 5000 friars at the Chapter of Mats (CE); two autographs (Robinson); age 44 ('forty-fifth year of his age', CE); Greccio 'about fifteen days before'; Fonte Colombo and 29 November 1223 (CE).

Feasts read in the calendar texts: 4 October in the Calendarium Romanum 1969 and USCCB; 17 September in the 1916 Martyrology and its 1969 relegation to particular calendars ('geminat ... memoriam S. Francisci'); 25 May translation (1916 Martyrology); 3 October in LFF 2022 (4 October blank); 4 October in the Church of England and ELCA ('renewer of the church'); absent from the LSB list.

Attributions: Jacques de Vitry and Elias in Sabatier (Houghton); Sabatier's pious-fraud and 'unique fact' passages; the 1237 bulls (Confessor Domini, and two to the bishop of Olmuetz and the Dominicans); Osipov ('well known in psychiatry ... nothing supernatural'); the OCA answer; Tamassia's charge as Howell reports it; Hallam as Okey quotes him; Okey's Fra Lupo and the Little Flowers 'compiled some time after 1322'; the Mirror of Perfection (about 1318) on the Podesta and the bishop; the Imitation's use of Admonition 20 (Robinson's footnote); Robinson's own words that his Canticle renders the original literally.

Rufino's touch of the side wound is 1 Cel 95, as cited; Honorius III is named in 1 Cel 73; birds at Bevagna, 'doves, rooks' (1 Cel 58); the coin in the mouth (2 Cel 65); the seven snow figures (2 Cel 117); Brother Ass pardoned (CE).

Rules: capitals for God in every quotation and in our text; no section marks; italicize.mjs dry run reports nothing; seo title 63 and description 156 characters; the 'Who' answer 58 words; number tiles read on their own and none is a slight.

Pictures: all four licences read through the Commons API (San_Francesco.jpg, StFrancis_part.jpg, Giotto._Predella_3.jpg, Bonaventura_Berlinghieri_Francesco.jpg: public domain, CC-PD-Mark); sizes match the data; nothing violent, no nudity; the hub card is centred on Cimabue's face with the eyes at about 37%.
changed: 'What others said' lede and the miracles lede: Celano wrote the First Life after the canonisation, 'between [16 July 1228] and February, 1229 ... by commission of Pope Gregory IX' (Howell), not 'for his canonisation'. Now 'at the bidding of Pope Gregory IX'; the miracles lede says it ends with the healings at the tomb (1 Cel 121, 127 on).

The leper moment: 1 Cel 17 says that when he looked at lepers' houses about two miles off he stopped his nostrils; the page had him holding his nose as he passed their houses. Now 'Even when he saw their houses two miles off, he held his nose.'

The 'Hidden' wound scene cited 1 Cel 95 but called the marks 'black' (a detail from the death scene, 1 Cel 113). Now follows 95: nails made of his own flesh, round heads on one side and bent points on the other.
Fonte Colombo: 'too loose to hold them' replaced by the CE's reason, 'too lengthy and unprecise to become a formal rule'.
Wolf myth: the Second Life (1244 to 1247) is 18 to 21 years after his death, so 'within twenty years' became 'about twenty years after his death'.
Doubt panel: added Howell's own verdict on Tamassia ('insufficient to establish his case'), so the charge is not left standing without the reply.
'Is he a saint?': the OCA answer speaks of stigmata in general (its example is Padre Pio), so 'stigmata such as his' became 'stigmata'.
for_owner: Group filter 'monks' for a friar (the writer's call; Nicholas has no group).
Hallam's 'hardly of sane mind' as the last voice in 'What others said' (quoted by Okey to disagree).
The band is 1104 x 1152 (the only large clear scan of Cimabue's face); the Subiaco portrait is 735 x 1024 and faded; Berlinghieri's panel is a small scan (the sharp photographs are CC BY-SA).
The Sultan's name rests on standard history, not a fetched text (circle card only).
